ai_industry.title: Google needs Hollywood more than the studios need AI
ai_industry.summary_original: Google has reportedly been reaching out to a number of Hollywood's biggest studios, hoping to strike licensing agreements that would allow it to train its AI models on copyrighted material in exchange for massive piles of cash. In theory, these deals would be…
ai_industry.content_original:
Google has reportedly been reaching out to a number of Hollywood’s biggest studios, hoping to strike licensing agreements that would allow it to train its AI models on copyrighted material in exchange for massive piles of cash. In theory, these deals would be a win-win: a huge financial boon to the studios that would also give Google a significant advantage in its race to outpace other AI companies. But while there’s little downside for Google, these deals pose a distinct set of risks to each of the studios that might be thinking about going all-in on AI. Getting into bed with Google this way might benefit Hollywood in the short term, but it could just as easily backfire and leave the public feeling burned by the entertainment industry.
Google needs Hollywood more than the studios need AI
Striking deals with studios like Disney could help the tech giant shift the narrative about artificial intelligence.
Though Google has not yet been able to get Disney, Warner Bros. Discovery, or Universal to agree to anything officially, the company’s executives have been reaching out to multiple studio representatives with pitches focused on its AI technology, according to unnamed sources speaking to The Los Angeles Times. Google wants permission to train its AI models on the studios’ vast libraries of copyrighted content, and it’s willing to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to get ahold of them. Per The LA Times, Google could pay a studio like Disney / Pixar around $40 million just for the rights to generate outputs featuring a single copyrighted character. That payout could swell well into the billions the more characters Google’s deals encompass, and studios might be able to secure a portion of however much advertising revenue Google makes from AI-generated content featuring that IP on platforms like YouTube.
As expensive as these partnerships would be for Google, they would also be an invaluable tool as the company continues to crystalize its position as one of the most prominent players in the AI game. Gemini being able to spit out Disney-approved images of Darth Vader and Snow White might not seem all that significant on its face, but that’s exactly the sort of thing that could get more ordinary, non tech-obsessed people seeing generative AI in a more positive (if innocuous) light. After years of hearing AI companies boast about their plans to disrupt society and eliminate jobs, public sentiment — especially among young people — about the technology has shifted into the negative. Even with tools like ChatGPT being as popular as they are, the larger AI industry has been so mired in controversy and plagued by concerns about its real world harms that it would now be hard-pressed to put out products that would immediately curry widespread goodwill. Striking deals with film and TV studios would give Google a convenient way to shift the larger narrative about its AI ambitions.
The content developed through these partnerships would presumably look better than the slop currently being churned out by models trained on ill-gotten source data, and having Google’s name and logos slapped all over official AI-generated Disney content would do wonders to legitimize this technology in people’s minds. But even if it didn’t, the partnership would still signal to the public that the entertainment industry sees generative AI as a tool worth embracing. It’s hard to quantify how valuable that framing would be to Google, whose DeepMind arm struck a $75 million investment deal with A24 earlier this summer. But it’s very easy to imagine how taking Google’s AI cash could put studios on a path that ultimately alienates their workers and audiences.
Regardless of whether a studio were to incorporate AI tools into their production workflows or simply feature user-generated AI content on their platforms (which was Disney and OpenAI’s plan before their partnership collapsed), striking a licensing agreement with Google would be a watershed moment.
Lionsgate, a notable studio but not a major player, struck a licensing deal with Runway in 2024. So far, nothing concrete has come out of that partnership, but the companies say they’re working on a plan to release AI-generated shorts. Once any one of the big legacy studios hop on to the AI bandwagon and manage to actually make something they can show the world, more production houses have a reason to follow suit. AI’s potential to speed production timelines up while keeping costs down is one of the main things that has kept studios interested in utilizing the technology. Shareholders would absolutely love it if production houses could put out more movies while spending less money, but doing that by using AI tools would almost certainly put a significant portion of the entertainment workforce out of jobs.
What may be keeping Disney and other studios from rushing to take Google up on its offers is the way that people have reacted to seeing AI used in the production of films like Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Fans were dismayed to find AI-generated images in Brand New Day’s official artbook, and the negative reaction might have been even more intense had people known about the technology’s use before the film hit theaters. It’s impossible to know for sure whether awareness about AI’s presence in Brand New Day’s production would have kept it from making $2 billion at the box office. But it stands to reason that none of the studios is eager to be the first to learn what happens when they release a project that’s presented as being the product of Google’s AI tools.
Though Google has everything to gain from Hollywood embracing AI, the studios have to be mindful of how endorsing this technology could leave them out on a limb. And as much as Google might be presenting its products as the solution to all of the entertainment industry’s issues, the AI industry needs Hollywood more than Hollywood needs more slop.

ai_industry.title: Trump Administration Sides With OpenAI in Publishers’ Copyright Lawsuits
ai_industry.summary_original: The federal government says making AI companies pay for content used to train their models would undermine national security.
ai_industry.content_original:
The Trump administration has weighed in on a series of copyright disputes between news organizations and OpenAI, supporting the ChatGPT-maker’s position that its use of publishers’ content to train AI models constituted fair use.
The statement of interest of the United States (PDF) was filed Tuesday in a series of cases in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, including one initiated by The New York Times and another by Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company. Ziff Davis filed the suit in 2025, alleging OpenAI infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.
In its filing, the federal government said a ruling in publishers’ favor could hinder AI development, limit competition among AI firms and hurt the country’s competitiveness with foreign developers.
“Rules of law that make it significantly more difficult to develop a robust AI industry in the United States … threaten national security and give a competitive advantage to foreign adversaries who are not so encumbered,” the filing states.
Graham James, a spokesperson for The New York Times, told CNET in a statement that the administration is “siding with a handful of trillion-dollar AI companies” instead of American creators and that doing so undermines both creators and AI developers.
“Both AI and creators can thrive – AI companies simply need to pay fairly for the content that makes their products possible, as copyright law requires,” James said. “The Administration’s proposal to let companies take that content without permission or compensation would undermine the sustainability of the human-created content that a healthy society depends on, and which AI needs to function.”
CNET has reached out to representatives for OpenAI and Ziff Davis for comment.
The Times initiated the lawsuit at the end of 2023, a year after ChatGPT’s debut. In its initial complaint (PDF), the news organization said large language models, such as those that power ChatGPT, were built using content that included millions of its articles. That training constituted an effort to “free-ride” on the Times’ investment in journalism and create products that compete.
The government said it sees LLMs’ ability to help others compete with large media corporations as a positive development. It cited independent authors using AI models to generate images that might otherwise require a photographer or license, and LLMs directing users to “dissenting sources that offer contrary information or perspectives.”
“It is not in the public’s interest for the largest technology companies to have an oligopoly on LLM training due to licensing entry barriers that function primarily as large subsidies for old mainstream media companies,” the government stated.
Major media companies aren’t the only ones who’ve sued OpenAI over copyright infringement. Authors, including big names like George R.R. Martin, have also accused the company of using their works in model training. OpenAI rival Anthropic, which makes Claude, settled piracy claims with authors for $1.5 billion, although a judge ruled the company’s use of copyrighted material was fair use.
Earlier this summer, publishers accused OpenAI of withholding evidence about how it trains its models, claims the company has denied.

ai_industry.title: Yearn for the Tern: Apple Has a New Daddy
ai_industry.summary_original: John Ternus takes the helm of a $4 trillion tech giant, but it comes with challenges as Apple faces down the RAM shortage, AI launch delays and the foldable phone market.
ai_industry.content_original:
John Ternus took over as Apple CEO on Tuesday, succeeding Tim Cook after serving as the company’s senior vice president of hardware engineering. His first day comes just over a week before the annual iPhone launch event on Sept. 9.
Under Cook, Apple became a $4 trillion company with an impressive, world-changing lineup of tech products, including every iPhone from 2012’s iPhone 5 onward, the Apple Watch, the AirPods, the Vision Pro and the HomePod, and services including Apple Music, Apple TV Plus and Apple Fitness Plus.
But what exactly is Ternus walking into? There are major challenges ahead, driven by the global RAM shortage, increasing smartphone competition and Apple’s struggles to keep up with the artificial intelligence race.
Farewell to Tim Cook
Cook, who took over as CEO two months before Apple co-founder Steve Jobs passed away in 2011, reportedly held a farewell party at Apple Park last weekend to cap off his 15 years at the helm of the company. Around 200 people — mostly Apple employees, but also Cook’s partner and the band OneRepublic — attended the party, according to The Information, citing unnamed sources.
Ternus reportedly spoke at the event, along with Steve Jobs’ widow, Laurene Powell Jobs; Apple’s former COO, Jeff Williams; and head of Apple Services and Health, Eddy Cue.
According to that report, anonymous sources have said the transition from Cook to Ternus should be one of continuity rather than upheaval, with many things expected to stay the same.
During his final earnings call as CEO in July, Cook praised Ternus, saying, “There is no better person to take the helm of the company.” He also called Ternus “brilliant and wonderful and capable” in his farewell note as Apple CEO on Monday.
“Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does, and I could not be more excited for his leadership,” Cook wrote this week.
With Ternus as CEO, Cook now serves as executive chair of Apple. Keeping him on in a senior role means Cook will still have influence over where Ternus decides to take Apple, and he could continue to be particularly influential with the current presidential administration, with which he’s fostered a good working relationship.
The Ternus takeover: Who is the new Apple CEO?
Ternus joined the tech giant back in 2001 as part of the product design team, having earned a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Pennsylvania and working as a mechanical engineer at Virtual Research Systems.
Rising through the ranks at Apple over 25 years, he became a VP of hardware engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021. Ternus worked across many flagship devices, including the iPad, AirPods, iPhone, Apple Watch and, most recently, the MacBook Neo. Apple also credits Ternus with improving device durability by incorporating 3D-printed titanium in the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and creating a recycled aluminum compound.
Ternus was last year tipped to be the frontrunner in the race to succeed Cook, and at 51, he’s around the same age Cook was when he took over as Apple CEO.
In Apple’s April announcement, Cook said Ternus “has the mind of an engineer, the soul of an innovator and the heart to lead with integrity and with honor.”
“Having spent almost my entire career at Apple, I have been lucky to have worked under Steve Jobs and to have had Tim Cook as my mentor,” Ternus said at the time.
IDC Worldwide Device Trackers senior research director Nabila Popal told CNET that she is “genuinely excited for Apple to go full circle and bring a products guy to lead Apple in this next phase, with an innovative lineup of interesting devices rumored to launch in the first few years of his leadership.”
The first two CEOs of Apple were likewise “products guys” — Michael Scott ran a semiconductor company, and Mike Markkula was an electrical engineer — so the choice of Ternus is a return to Apple’s roots.
The state of Apple in 2026: What is Ternus inheriting?
His takeover comes just over a week before Apple unveils its next set of products, likely including the long-rumored foldable iPhone and the iPhone 18 lineup — but there are challenges ahead, even with a highly anticipated product launch.
“We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal,” Ternus said in his letter to Apple employees Tuesday morning. “I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet that we’ll dream up and create together.”
One major test for Ternus will be the prices for the next iPhone, which are likely to have a higher price tag due to the ongoing global RAM shortage caused by the rapid expansion of AI tools. In June, Apple raised prices on over a dozen products across iPads, Macs and home devices.
“The September launch will be an important first test for John Ternus as CEO,” Counterpoint Research principal analyst Yang Wang told CNET. “A premium-focused lineup could strengthen Apple’s product mix, but it also increases the risk if pricing moves too far ahead of consumer demand.”
Most phones released this year have seen $100 bumps, including the Samsung Galaxy S26 line, while a few higher-end models have gone up $200 over their predecessors. Counterpoint projects the iPhone 18 lineup to see a price increase of $200-$250 per phone compared to the iPhone 17 lineup, “with high-spec models potentially seeing price hikes even beyond the range.”
Rumors suggest a standard iPhone 18 won’t be part of the lineup next week, instead launching in the spring alongside a potential iPhone 18E. This could extend the shelf life of the current iPhone 17, which is still seeing “strong demand” in 2026, according to Counterpoint Research. Typically, Apple discounts its previous model by $100 when a new iPhone is announced; if there’s no new base model, Apple can keep the iPhone 17 at its full price.
“Ternus knows the hardware organization very well, but the challenge will be balancing product ambition with affordability and launch execution,” Wang said, adding that he expects Samsung to overtake Apple for the global smartphone lead by the end of 2026.
The chip shortage across DRAM and NAND flash, which are needed for phones but are being gobbled up by AI data centers, is real. But there has been some criticism that tech giants are not shielding customers from chipflation despite seeing record sales; Apple, for instance, raked in roughly $109 billion in net sales and reported almost $30 billion in net income during the previous quarter.
At the end of August, analyst firm IDC said smartphone shipments are set for a record 17% drop this year due to the memory crisis, with NAND and DRAM costs up 300% compared to last year.
“The components that make AI possible are the same ones in short supply, and their cost is being passed straight through to the shelf,” IDC vice president for worldwide client devices Francisco Jeronimo wrote on Aug. 26. “Average selling prices are up 27.6% this year and will keep rising well into 2027. The era of the cheap smartphone has ended.”
According to IDC, “foldables remain the only silver lining.”
Could a foldable revitalize the iPhone?
Apple is late to the foldable phone game, assuming it finally launches one next week. Samsung is now on its eighth generation of foldable phones, with the recent launch of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Flip 8, which follow the company’s first foldable phone in 2019. There are also competitor folding phones such as Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold, Motorola’s Razr Fold and other Chinese options from Oppo, OnePlus and Huawei.
IDC is predicting “rapid growth” in the foldable phones market thanks to Apple’s expected entry into the sector. It forecasts Apple will ship more than 17 million foldable iPhones by next year, snatching 40% of the folding phone market share, potentially making it the dominant force over Samsung, Google and Huawei.

ai_industry.title: Can AI design circuit boards yet?
ai_industry.summary_original: A look at what current models can build, where they fail, and how EEBench tests the electronics in simulation.
ai_industry.content_original:
Can AI design circuit boards yet?
OpenAI showed GPT-6 Astra working in KiCad. We have been building a way to measure whether the circuits that come out of these models are any good.
We got pretty excited yesterday when OpenAI put a demo of GPT-6 Astra working on a circuit board in KiCad on the front page of its launch post. It is cool to see electronics show up in a major model release like this.
We are obviously still some distance from asking an AI to build an entire phone in one prompt. The demo does raise a question we have been thinking about for a while, though: how do we measure whether the electronics an AI produces are actually any good?
The models know a surprising amount about electronics
Our experience has been that current models know much more about electronics than their output in conventional design tools tends to show. They have read textbooks, datasheets, application notes and a lot of code.
You can have an agent operate a graphical CAD tool, but it spends a lot of time clicking around and keeping track of what is on screen. A lot of its context consists of coordinates, menus and application state.
EEBench uses atopile instead. The circuit lives in declarative code, so the agent can work directly on components, connections and electrical constraints. It can change the design, build it, run a simulation and inspect what failed without leaving the project.
This has worked much better for us than asking a model to draw lines in a GUI. It also means the benchmark can spend less time testing computer use and more time testing electronics.
The real world is messy
One of the public tasks is based on a residential energy meter. When its 5 V supply disappears, the circuit has to keep the processor alive for another 20 ms so it can save the accumulated reading. The protected rail must stay above the processor's 3.0 V brownout threshold during that window.
Most models intuitively jump to the right base conclusion: add a capacitor.
A real capacitor makes the task more interesting. A ceramic part may provide much less than its advertised capacitance once it has voltage across it. Parts have tolerances. Adding more capacitance costs more, takes up space and makes the rail slower to recharge when the power returns. A design that works with nominal values can fail with the parts that arrive.
EEBench cuts the input power in simulation and measures what happens. It checks the voltage throughout the outage, the effective capacitance at the operating point, the recovery after power returns and the limits on package, dielectric, voltage rating and cost.
The meter is one of the easier tasks. In a harder analog task, the agent may have to synthesize a multiple-feedback low-pass filter around an op-amp, solve the resistor and capacitor ratios for the required poles, and keep its gain, cutoff frequency and Q inside their limits after every component is pushed to a worst-case tolerance corner. The harness rebuilds the SPICE deck for those corners, runs the AC and transient captures, binds measurements to named probes, and records each result against its lower and upper specification limits.
But getting the equations right is only part of electronics engineering. EEBench uses real manufacturer parts, with specifications extracted from their datasheets and carried into the SPICE model. The agent has to find a combination that works across those tolerance corners while also choosing parts that exist, can be ordered and are reasonably priced for the product. That trade-off between electrical performance, cost and supply is much closer to designing real hardware than picking ideal values from a textbook.
This is the part we find most interesting, because it is what electrical engineering eventually boils down to, just like every other engineering discipline: trade-offs.
How the grading works
EEBench checks are fully deterministic. It builds the submitted design, constructs the circuit graph and bill of materials, and runs a set of SPICE simulations and design checks. Each requirement produces a measurement with a limit.
For the energy-meter task, the harness measures the protected rail while the input drops out and returns. Other tasks measure gain, thresholds, ripple, transient response and behavior at component-tolerance corners. The technical score is combined with cost efficiency against a reference bill of materials. Cost only helps once the circuit works.
This is similar to giving a coding agent a compiler and tests, except the tests are measuring voltages and component behavior..
EEBench V1 covers analog and digital design through simulation. It does not yet tell us whether a model can lay out, manufacture and bring up a complete product. We want to add those parts later. The current benchmark concentrates on the requirements, design and verification loop because that is where we can already grade useful engineering work objectively. The full methodology and sample result explorer are public.
What we are seeing on the leaderboard
The September 1 results are encouraging. Claude Opus 5 scored 61.6% across the 13 tasks in EEBench V1. Grok 4.6 came second at 57.1%, just ahead of Claude Fable 5.1 at 56.4%. A few months ago we would not have expected models to do this well.
There was another result we were especially happy to see: xAI included EEBench in the Grok 4.6 model card. It appears in the section on “engineering acceleration,” alongside evaluations for 3D modeling and parametric CAD. Their published run put Grok 4.6 at 60.0% with xhigh reasoning effort. Seeing a frontier lab use EEBench to describe a new model's engineering ability makes us think this is becoming a category people care about.
Anthropic's models have consistently done well in this environment. Grok's rise is also interesting. In its Grok 4.6 launch post, xAI says the model received high-quality engineering data and RL training in domain-specific environments including computer-aided design. Its EEBench result fits that story.
The OpenAI models we have tested so far sit further down the table. GPT-5.5 scored 42.3%, while GPT-5.6 Sol scored 39.4%. We do not have a GPT-6 Astra result yet. After seeing it work on a board in KiCad, we would really like to find out how it handles these circuit-design tasks.
Training environment
Once we had a simulation harness that could grade a circuit, we also had the beginnings of an RL environment for electronics. The same checks can be used as reward signals during post-training.
A failed run contains useful information. We can see which voltage missed its limit, which operating corner failed, or whether the model solved the problem with an unnecessarily expensive design. That gives a training loop more to work with than a model saying that a schematic looks plausible.
EEBench is the small, public view of this work. We are also starting to work directly with frontier labs that want to make their models better at electronics. If you work on evals or post-training, you can talk to us about the larger evaluation suites and simulation-backed training environments we provide.
So, can it design a circuit board?
For a useful and growing set of circuit problems, we think the answer is already yes. The scores also make it clear that there is plenty left to do. OpenAI choosing a PCB for one of Astra's first demos and xAI publishing EEBench in a model card both feel like early signs of the same thing: AI labs are starting to take electronics seriously.
There may be another data point very soon. Elon Musk has said that Grok 4.7 is coming within weeks after additional training on a large collection of SpaceX data, with the aim of making it especially good at engineering. The model is not out and the schedule may move, but if it arrives as described, we will be keen to put it on EEBench.

ai_industry.content_original:
Nvidia's controversial, face-changing, gen-AI DLSS 5 tech releases tomorrow for one game, and seems to tank frame-rates
"Together, these innovations mark the beginning of a transformative era."
Nvidia's hotly debated DLSS 5 tech, which uses generative AI to apply graphical filters to existing games, arrives this week, albeit only in one game. The game is NBA 2K7, and the GeForce drivers for DLSS 5 arrive Thursday night in the US (9pm PDT) and early Friday morning here (5am BST). This is only available for GeForce 50-series graphics cards, laptops and GeForce Now.
The big, controversial part of DLSS 5 is "neural rendering", which goes beyond DLSS's previous remit of improving game performance "to transform visual fidelity as well", Nvidia wrote in a blog post. "While previous DLSS technologies focused on reconstructing existing scene data to deliver higher-resolution images, additional frames, or cleaner ray-traced lighting, DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering takes the next step by using AI to generate the rich lighting and material details that real-time performance constraints once forced developers to strip away, allowing them to realise their original artistic vision.
"Instead of generating frames from text prompts, 3D-Guided Neural Rendering uses the game engine's rendered frame, complete with its artist-designed geometry, textures, and lighting buffers, as an unyielding foundation. DLSS 5 becomes the final rendering stage of the graphics pipeline, infusing scenes with lifelike lighting and materials while ensuring the engine frame defines what must remain, and the artist directs what may change."
It was examples of DLSS 5 helping developers "realise their original artistic vision" that were widely criticised earlier this year, when Nvidia shared images of Resident Evil Requiem main character Grace Ashcroft altered by neural rendering in DLSS 5. Her face appeared noticeably changed, and not necessarily in a good way; calls of "yassifying" her face - or artificially beautifying it according to skewed social media-filtered standards - were rife.
A slew of DLSS 5-altered game characters' faces also appeared this past weekend as the technology leaked ahead of release. Modders tried the technology in Remedy's Control, and also experimented with DLSS 5 in GTA 5, Cyberpunk 2077, and The Witcher 3. Geralt certainly looks a lot older.
Nvidia's latest blog explained the neural rendering process in more detail, using subtler example images this time, while also underlining issues such as 'preserving artistic intent' and the control developers and players have to use DLSS 5 a little or a lot, or not at all. You can simply turn it off. A couple of 'before and after' screenshots of NBA 2K7 show basketball players Cade Cunningham and Tyrese Haliburton lit with, what appears to me, more realistic lighting.
But there's not only an ethical gen-AI-related concern to turning this on but, reportedly, a performance one as well. DLSS 5 - ironically for what was previously a performance-enhancing technology - seems to drastically affect frame-rates. It might not look like it in the blog, because the graphs there boast high frame rates, but as PC Gamer pointed out, they are based on 6x multi-frame generation numbers - ie. they've been multiplied by six. Reverse that and it's a different story.
Suddenly, a GeForce RTX 5060 card in a good machine only runs NBA 2K7 in 1080p on Ultra settings at 43 FPS, and a shiny GeForce RTX 5090 just breaks 60 FPS in 4K on Ultra. Still, it's better than the two 5090s the blog says it took to run DLSS 5 back in March, when it was announced. "Since the initial announcement of DLSS 5 in March, our progress has been rapid: from running on dual GeForce RTX 5090s to now a single graphics card, we've achieved a 5X performance gain in just six months," Nvidia wrote, "making DLSS 5 available for all GeForce RTX 50 Series GPUs and Laptop GPUs.
"Our optimisation curve isn't flattening out, and we have further optimisations in active development. We expect upcoming model updates coming in the [autumn] to boost performance beyond today's baseline. Backed by over a decade of DLSS expertise, we remain committed to continuously pushing the boundaries of performance and image quality, and this is only the beginning.
"Together, these innovations mark the beginning of a transformative era which blends hand-crafted rendering with neural graphics to deliver a dramatic leap in visual realism while preserving the control artists need for creative expression."
